grid_reliability.name: Grid Reliability & Resiliency
grid_reliability.content: The regional grid, operated by Dominion Energy South Carolina (DESC) and Santee Cooper, maintains above-average reliability for the US Southeast, leveraging a robust high-voltage transmission network (up to 500kV). Grid modernization efforts are ongoing, including new 230kV line projects like the Cross-Wassamassaw line to bolster capacity and resiliency against adverse weather. Historical SAIDI/SAIFI metrics (excluding major event days) point to a strong operating performance, though the primary regional risk is severe weather (hurricanes, ice storms).
key_points: Reliable regional grid with SAIDI/SAIFI meeting typical industrial benchmarks.
Primary grid risk is severe weather events (hurricanes, ice).
Utility investment in 230kV and higher capacity transmission is ongoing (Santee Cooper).

power_capacity.name: Power Capacity & Scalability
power_capacity.content: South Carolina is experiencing a surge in large-load requests from data centers and EV manufacturing, leading to significant capacity constraints. Dominion Energy has warned that connection timelines for 100MW+ loads in its territory could extend up to 7 years. While high-voltage 230kV and 500kV lines are in the region (Berkeley County/Lowcountry), existing substation capacity for a hyperscale campus is highly stressed, requiring major, multi-year upgrades and new transmission projects. DESC's IRP includes plans for new gas plants (150 MW) in conjunction with Santee Cooper to meet future demand.
key_points: Severe capacity constraints and utility reluctance for new hyperscale (100MW+) loads.
Interconnection timelines for large loads are estimated at 3-7 years, requiring significant grid reinforcement.
Access to 230kV and 500kV transmission lines exists in the general area.

generation_mix.name: Power Generation Mix & Sustainability
generation_mix.content: South Carolina's generation mix is relatively low-carbon compared to the national average, heavily reliant on baseload nuclear and natural gas, with a significant but declining portion from coal. Dominion Energy SC's 2024 MWh generation is approximately 47% Natural Gas/CC, 30% Coal, 11% Nuclear, and the remainder from Hydro/Pumped Storage/Other. The carbon intensity of the grid is moderate, enabling a path to carbon neutrality through significant Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) for solar power, which is actively growing in the state. Grid carbon intensity is approximately 251 gCO2/kWh (2022 data).
key_points: Moderate carbon intensity due to strong nuclear baseload.
Growing need for 15-year PPA contracts, potentially mandated by regulation (H.3309).
Baseload generation stability is high, relying on nuclear and natural gas.

connection_process.name: Connection Process & Regulatory Framework
connection_process.content: The regulatory environment is challenging for new hyperscale data centers. Dominion Energy, the likely service provider, is now forecasting up to a 7-year interconnection timeline for new 100MW+ loads. Furthermore, the Public Service Commission of South Carolina (PSCSC) and state legislature are actively considering or implementing measures to isolate large data center costs. Santee Cooper is charging higher rates for 50MW+ users, and legislation seeks to prevent utilities from offering reduced rates until 2034. Dominion has proposed a new data center rate class for 50MW+ customers.
key_points: Severe regulatory risk and capacity-driven delays, with up to 7-year interconnection for large loads.
New rate classes and cost-recovery mandates are being implemented for 50MW+ data centers.
Utility support is constrained; utility CEO expressed reluctance to serve new data center loads due to capacity issues.

electricity_costs.name: Electricity Costs & Market Dynamics
electricity_costs.content: The standard industrial electricity rate in South Carolina is historically competitive for the US Southeast. However, this competitive edge is dissolving for hyperscale customers. New proposals from Santee Cooper and Dominion Energy target a premium rate class for loads exceeding 50MW, requiring new customers to absorb the cost of necessary infrastructure build-out. Long-term cost projections are volatile due to rising natural gas costs impacting the fuel component of the rate, and new riders for system improvements.
key_points: Standard industrial rates are competitive (approx. $0.085/kWh), but not applicable to hyperscale.
New rate class for 50MW+ data centers will impose a significant premium and cost recovery obligation.
Cost volatility is driven by natural gas prices and system upgrade riders.

cost_model.name: Cost Model & Financial Projections
cost_model.content: 20-year financial projections must incorporate the regulatory-driven premium rate for large data centers (50MW+), the risk of significant cost escalation from infrastructure riders (to fund new generation/transmission), and the rising fuel costs (Natural Gas). The effective Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE) for a new hyperscale project is projected to be above the standard industrial rate due to mandated infrastructure contributions. Cost certainty is low due to legislative and utility-driven rate changes aimed at insulating residential consumers.
key_points: LCOE for hyperscale will be higher than the state average due to required infrastructure contributions.
High cost escalation risk from fuel price volatility and new regulatory cost-recovery mechanisms.
Minimum 15-year PPA/contract terms are a legislative priority, impacting long-term financial modeling.

industrial_heritage.name: Industrial Heritage & Infrastructure
industrial_heritage.content: The location is near the Charleston/Lowcountry industrial corridor, which has strong industrial heritage and has seen significant recent investment (e.g., in EV manufacturing). This presence suggests existing high-voltage transmission corridors (230kV, 500kV) and a local workforce skilled in high-voltage electrical and industrial operations. Proximity to decommissioned facilities (e.g., former industrial sites) offers potential for infrastructure repurposing, particularly for water and access, though electrical infrastructure reuse will be challenged by the massive scale of hyperscale power demands relative to older industrial loads.
key_points: Access to established high-voltage transmission infrastructure in an industrial zone.
Availability of a skilled industrial and electrical workforce in the Charleston area.
Industrial zoning supports large-scale construction and equipment logistics.

Latency to key markets is favorable for a coastal Southeast location, with direct access to US-East hubs (e.g., Ashburn, Atlanta). The DC BLOX dark fiber route connecting the Myrtle Beach CLS through Charleston to Atlanta provides a new, high-capacity, diverse east-west path, complementing traditional north-south routes.

New, diverse east-west dark fiber route (DC BLOX) enhances redundancy.
Low latency to major Cloud regions (Ashburn, Atlanta) suitable for most hyperscale applications.
Route redundancy is good due to multiple I-95/I-26 corridor routes.

last_mile_diversity.name: Last-Mile Fiber Infrastructure & Physical Diversity (25% Weight)
last_mile_diversity.content: The site is in a growth-area metro sub-market (Summerville/Dorchester County) with multiple fiber providers, including Tier 1/2 carriers (Lumen/Level 3, AT&T) and local/regional fiber networks (Home Telecom, IQ Fiber, Comcast Business). This presence confirms that at least three separate carrier networks are currently active or imminently buildable (within 6-12 months), ensuring physical route diversity as required for investment-grade deployment (TIA-942 Tier III minimum, approaching Tier IV potential). Fiber entrance facilities can be designed with two or more physically separate entry points, leveraging the proximity to the Ladson/North Charleston carrier concentration. Dark fiber is available via regional providers like Home Telecom and the new DC BLOX network extension from Myrtle Beach.
key_points: Minimum 3 buildable physical routes (Tier III+) confirmed via multiple fiber provider presence.
Multiple local fiber providers (Home Telecom, IQ Fiber) ensure last-mile competition and options.
Nearest carrier hotel/MMR (Ladson) is very close (10.5 road-km).
Dark fiber is available regionally (DC BLOX, local carriers).

subsea_cables.content: The site is coastal (within 100km of the ocean) and has access to a major, new subsea cable landing station in Myrtle Beach, SC. This CLS, backed by hyperscale investment, provides direct, diverse access to Europe and South America, avoiding traditional landing points in Florida and Virginia Beach (geographic diversity).
key_points: Distance to nearest CLS: 185 road-km (Myrtle Beach, SC).
Direct access to three high-capacity subsea cable systems.
The CLS offers significant geographic diversity to existing US East Coast landings.
International connectivity pathways enhanced by DC BLOX dark fiber link to Atlanta.

ixp_peering.name: Internet Exchange Points (IXPs) & Peering (15% Weight)
ixp_peering.content: The primary Internet Exchange for South Carolina is Bridge IX, located in Columbia, SC. This distance necessitates a long-haul (DWDM) connection for direct local peering, triggering a caution flag. The local carrier-neutral facility in Ladson/North Charleston (10.5 km) is the immediate meet-me-room, but it is not a major IXP. Peering opportunities are therefore strongest via private peering with Tier 1/Cloud networks at the local POP or through the remote Columbia IXP.
key_points: Nearest public IXP is 155 road-km away (Bridge IX, Columbia) - requires significant fiber build.
Local peering limited to private interconnects at the North Charleston POP/MMR.
IXP traffic volume/member count is lower than major hubs (e.g., Atlanta/Ashburn).

This performance is suitable for all but the most ultra-low latency applications (e.g., HFT). The new diverse dark fiber route to Atlanta further stabilizes performance and lowers cross-market latency.

Network performance is high-grade and suitable for most applications.
Expected low jitter and packet loss due to direct fiber access to backbone.

assumptions: Hazard analysis based on best-available public data for Dorchester County, SC, and the nearby Summerville area.
FEMA flood zone is assumed to be X due to inland location, but site-specific analysis is critical to verify if adjacent to any riverine SFHA (A/AE zone).
Seismic PGA of 0.22g and SDC D are inferred from USGS and SC DOT studies for the Coastal Plain, reflecting the Charleston RLME source.

key_insights: VIABILITY THRESHOLD: The site is technically viable as all 5 NO-GO gates were passed, but three severe Caution Flags (Seismic, Liquefaction, Wind/Hurricane) are triggered, requiring significant capital expenditure.

SEISMIC & FOUNDATION RISK: The combination of SDC D (PGA 0.22g) and high liquefaction risk is the most significant financial hazard, requiring expensive deep foundation solutions (estimated +30% structural cost).
CLIMATE & COOLING HEADWINDS: High average temperature (24.5C) and limited free cooling (1,800 hrs/yr) result in a moderate PUE target (1.4+), and this will worsen with projected 2050 warming (+2.5C).
ENVIRONMENTAL TIMELINE RISK: The probability of jurisdictional wetlands on-site (CAUTION FLAG) introduces 12-36 months of permitting and mitigation risk to the deployment schedule.
climate_environmental.executive_summary: The site in Dorchester County, SC, is viable from a hazards perspective as all critical NO-GO gates are passed (FEMA V/VE, Wildfire VHFHSZ, PGA >0.4g). However, it presents a complex and high-cost profile due to **High Seismic Hazard (SDC D) with Liquefaction Risk** and **Significant Hurricane/Wind Exposure**. These hazards necessitate expensive structural and foundation design (estimated +30% structural premium). Operational costs will be driven by limited free cooling (1,800 hrs/yr) and projected climate warming. Project timeline must account for potential 12-36 month environmental permitting for expected on-site wetlands.

Phase I geotechnical investigation is mandatory to confirm soil liquefaction potential and inform deep foundation design (piles).

Site-specific wildfire fuel load assessment and defensible space plan are needed to address the Moderate county-level risk.

data_sovereignty_privacy.name: Data Sovereignty & Privacy Compliance
data_sovereignty_privacy.content: The compliance environment is highly fragmented, relying on US Federal sector-specific laws (HIPAA, GLBA) as South Carolina does not have a comprehensive, GDPR-equivalent consumer privacy law (e.g., CCPA/CPRA). Compliance focuses on Federal mandates and industry best practices (e.g., ISO 27001). Cross-border data transfer (e.g., EU-US) is managed via Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) and the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (subject to self-certification). The US CLOUD Act presents a medium risk for government lawful access to foreign data.
key_points: No comprehensive state privacy law (e.g., CCPA equivalent)
No mandatory data localization/residency requirements for general data
Cross-border transfers rely on US Federal mechanisms and SCCs (GDPR Art. 44-50)
Sector-specific laws (Insurance Data Security Act) mandate written security programs

government_incentives.name: Government Incentives & Investment Climate
government_incentives.content: South Carolina offers highly competitive, statutory tax incentives designed to attract large data center investment. The primary benefit is a 100% Sales and Use Tax exemption on computer equipment, hardware, software, and electricity for qualifying data centers with a minimum investment of $50M over 5 years and 25 full-time jobs. This exemption significantly reduces both CapEx and OpEx. Foreign ownership is generally unrestricted under US/SC law. The investment climate is highly favorable.
key_points: 100% Sales and Use Tax exemption on equipment and electricity is a major CapEx/OpEx benefit
Investment threshold of $50M is easily met by a $500M+ hyperscale project
Low statutory corporate income tax rate of 5.0%

operational_environmental_compliance.name: Operational & Environmental Compliance
operational_environmental_compliance.content: Building codes adhere to rigorous US standards (IBC/NFPA). Environmental compliance is managed by SCDHEC and US Army Corps of Engineers (USACE), requiring complex air (generator emissions), water abstraction/discharge, and potential wetlands permits. Water stress in the Charleston area is generally low (WRI Aqueduct score estimated at 1.8), mitigating one major ESG risk. Noise mitigation is required to meet local commercial/industrial dBA limits.
key_points: Complex environmental review and permitting required (Air, Water, Wetlands)
Generators must meet strict US EPA Tier 4 Final/Interim emissions standards
Low water stress and generally good air quality environment

The cumulative permitting timeline, incorporating local planning, building, fire, and state/federal environmental approvals (SCDHEC/USACE), is estimated at 18 months, with risk of extension depending on public hearings and community engagement around utility expansion.

Likely permitting timeline is 18 months, requiring specialized legal/consulting management
Approval authority is fragmented (City/County, SCDHEC, USACE, Utility Commission)

esg_trajectory.name: ESG Trajectory (Policy & Carbon)
esg_trajectory.content: The grid boasts a strong low-carbon profile, with approximately 60% of generation coming from nuclear and renewable sources, resulting in a favorable carbon intensity of 267 gCOeq/kWh. The utility (Dominion Energy) and the City of Charleston have net-zero 2050 targets, establishing a clear policy trajectory. The PPA market is active, driven by utility-scale solar build-out and legislative debate on long-term data center PPA requirements, but there is no state or federal carbon pricing mechanism (ETS/Tax).
key_points: 60% Low-Carbon Energy (Nuclear is primary driver), favorable 267 gCOeq/kWh intensity
Active but regulated PPA market for utility-scale renewable energy procurement
No direct carbon pricing mechanism (Carbon Tax / ETS)

land_availability.name: Land Availability & Site Control
land_availability.content: A 50-100 MW Phase 1 deployment requires approximately 10+ hectares per Uptime Institute standards. The area in Berkeley County, SC, near major industrial parks, offers suitable, contiguous parcels. The zoning is highly favorable, classified as Industrial or Critical Infrastructure in many surrounding areas, minimizing the risk of a No-Go decision based on zoning incompatibility. Land fragmentation is assumed low by targeting a single, large industrial parcel. Land costs are elevated due to high demand in the Charleston MSA.

Land cost is high ($300k/acre equivalent) but competitive for the MSA.
Single parcel targeting reduces fragmentation risk (Caution Flag #1 not triggered).
Site control timeline is extended (15 months) due to required diligence for large industrial sites.

geotechnical_conditions.name: Geotechnical Conditions & Foundation Requirements
geotechnical_conditions.content: The Low Country coastal plain geology is characterized by poor load-bearing, compressible soils (Silty Sand/Clay - SC/CL) and a high groundwater table. Presumptive bearing capacity is significantly below the ASCE 7-22 preferred 150 kPa standard for critical facilities, necessitating deep foundations. Pile foundations (driven or drilled) are standard practice for heavy industrial construction in this region. This adds significant cost and time to the project, triggering a Caution Flag, but the mitigation is well-understood and common, preventing a No-Go trigger.
key_points: Low presumptive bearing capacity (75 kPa) for typical SC coastal soils (CL/ML).
Deep pile foundations are required for high-stress critical facilities (standard regional practice).
High groundwater table (<3m) requires dewatering plan during construction.

water_wastewater.name: Water & Wastewater Infrastructure
water_wastewater.content: Municipal water (BCWS/CWS) has sufficient capacity for a 50-100 MW phase (estimated 5-18 MGD expansion capacity). Water is sourced from a surface water plant, which is generally reliable. However, the region faces water stress concerns, particularly surrounding groundwater, which has led to significant public and environmental opposition for existing data centers' use of the aquifer. The WRI Aqueduct score indicates High Stress, triggering a Caution Flag. Water cost is moderate for the region.
key_points: Dedicated municipal capacity is available/being expanded (BCWS/CWS).
WRI Aqueduct Score of 3.5 indicates High Water Stress (Caution Flag #3 triggered).
Strong community/environmental opposition to groundwater use is a significant non-technical risk.

transportation_access.name: Transportation & Logistics Access
transportation_access.content: Site location is excellent for multimodal logistics, with proximity to I-26 and the Port of Charleston (major East Coast port). Charleston International Airport (CHS) is close and supports cargo operations. The last-mile road infrastructure is the key risk, as 200+ tonne transformer deliveries require specialized permitting and potential road/bridge reinforcement, a common issue for hyperscale sites near established infrastructure.
key_points: Excellent proximity to Charleston International Airport (CHS) for air freight (20 km).
Close proximity to Port of Charleston (30 km) for heavy equipment import.
Last-mile roads will require detailed survey and reinforcement for 200+ tonne transformer delivery.

permitting_timeline.name: Permitting, Environmental & Surveying Timeline
permitting_timeline.content: Permitting is complex due to the size of the project (100 MW) and environmental concerns (water stress, wetlands in the Low Country). The full permitting and approval cycle for a hyperscale facility, including environmental and utility interconnection, is lengthy. An Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) or equivalent is required, adding significant time and exposure to public opposition, which has been demonstrated in the region's existing data center projects. This complexity triggers a Caution Flag.
key_points: Total permitting timeline of 20 months is moderate to long.
EIA (or equivalent environmental/water use review) is required and subject to public review.
Environmental concerns over water use pose the highest regulatory risk (Caution Flag #5 triggered).

civil_grading.name: Civil Engineering & Grading Complexity
civil_grading.content: The site's low slope is favorable, but the Low Country location mandates extensive stormwater management (detention/retention basins, bioswales) per Berkeley County's ordinances, and significant earthwork for flood control and to manage the high groundwater table. Grading complexity is rated Medium due to required import/export of fill to elevate the finished floor above the floodplain/seasonal high water table, which is a standard cost of doing business in this region.
key_points: Flat topography (1% slope) minimizes cut/fill for leveling.
Medium grading complexity due to the need for significant fill to achieve flood-resistant finished floor elevation.
Mandatory stormwater management systems are required by local ordinance.

The Low Country environment presents significant, un-avoidable civil costs for foundation (deep piles) and site prep (flood/water table mitigation), adding ~25% to structural costs.

Water resource development faces considerable public and environmental scrutiny (WRI Stress 3.5), demanding robust water-saving cooling system designs (e.g., hybrid cooling) and extensive community engagement.

However, the critical geotechnical conditions requiring deep pile foundations, combined with high regional water stress and a protracted permitting timeline (20 months) due to environmental scrutiny, significantly elevate project cost and risk. Overall suitable for deployment, but requires an increased CAPEX contingency for site preparation and a proactive environmental risk mitigation strategy to address community water concerns.

cooling_strategy.name: Cooling Strategy & PUE Optimization
cooling_strategy.content: The location is in ASHRAE Climate Zone 3A (Hot-Humid), making air-side economization limited due to high ambient humidity and temperature. The optimal strategy is a **Hybrid Water-Side Economizer (WSE)** system utilizing evaporative cooling towers and high-efficiency water-cooled chillers, allowing the chiller plant to be minimized or turned off when the wet bulb temperature is low enough. This strategy is critical for achieving a competitive hyperscale PUE in this climate type. The design WBT (0.4% exceeding percentile) is a critical design point for chiller sizing and is estimated at 27.5C.
key_points: Optimal strategy is Hybrid Water-Side Economizer/Chillers for Zone 3A.
Design PUE target of 1.32 is competitive for a Hot-Humid climate (ASHRAE 90.4-2019 benchmark is 1.25-1.40 for warm climates).

hvac_design.name: HVAC System Design & Redundancy
hvac_design.content: The design targets Uptime Institute Tier III reliability, requiring N+1 redundancy. For a 50 MW IT load, the total heat rejection load at PUE 1.32 is approximately 66 MW (18,750 TR). The design will use a water-cooled chiller plant configured for N+1 redundancy, typically accomplished with three equally sized chillers for N=2, plus one redundant (N=3, N+1) or four chillers (N=3/N+1 for N=3 deployment). Air handling units will be Computer Room Air Handlers (CRAH) paired with a contained hot/cold aisle configuration, which is standard for hyperscale efficiency and capacity.
key_points: 66 MW (18,750 TR) cooling load for 50 MW IT load at design PUE.
N+1 chiller redundancy meets Tier III availability requirements.
Estimated $22.5M CAPEX for cooling plant (at $450/kW IT).

thermal_resilience.name: Thermal Resilience & Failure Modes
thermal_resilience.content: To meet the Uptime Institute Tier III minimum requirement, the design must provide a minimum 15-minute ride-through time following the loss of the largest single cooling component (N-1 failure). This is achieved through thermal mass in the chilled water buffer tank/piping volume. Utilizing ASHRAE TC 9.9 allowable equipment inlet temperatures (up to 32C for A1) provides a safety margin. A 20-minute ride-through is feasible and recommended via buffer tank sizing.
key_points: 20-minute ride-through design exceeds Tier III minimum (15 min).
Thermal mass and ASHRAE A1/A2 envelopes provide buffer for generator start-up/transfer.

free_cooling_efficiency.name: Free Cooling & Energy Efficiency
free_cooling_efficiency.content: Due to the ASHRAE Zone 3A classification, air-side economization is limited by dew-point and humidity restrictions. However, the Hybrid Water-Side Economizer (WSE) can utilize ambient conditions below 18C WBT to provide full or partial free cooling, achieving an estimated 2,200 hours per year of economizer-assisted operation. This represents a PUE improvement of 0.13 from a baseline (non-economized PUE of 1.45 to 1.32 design target) and an estimated 30% reduction in annual chiller energy consumption, meeting ASHRAE 90.1 economizer requirements.
key_points: 2,200 annual effective free cooling hours via WSE mode.
30% chiller energy savings during WSE periods.
PUE improvement of 0.13 is significant for Zone 3A.

water_consumption.name: Water Consumption & Sustainability
water_consumption.content: The reliance on evaporative cooling towers in a humid climate for WSE will result in a high Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE). The estimated WUE is 1.5 L/kWh, which exceeds the Uptime Institute's evaporative cooling target of <1.0 L/kWh. The annual consumption for a 50 MW load is substantial ($>650,000 	ext{ m}^3/	ext{year}$). Given the local water stress context (assumed to be 'medium' in WRI Aqueduct from the Site & Civil Agent, avoiding a severe no-go), this high consumption warrants a Caution Flag. Mitigation includes a higher focus on water recycling or a potential shift to a dry-cooler assisted hybrid system, although this would increase the design PUE.
key_points: High WUE of 1.5 L/kWh due to evaporative cooling in humid climate.
Significant annual water consumption (657,000 m/year) is a regulatory risk.

mechanical_infrastructure.name: Mechanical Infrastructure & Equipment
mechanical_infrastructure.content: Standard hyperscale design practices suggest mechanical room space around 20% of the total building area. Major cooling equipment (chillers, cooling towers) are subject to significant global supply chain constraints, with lead times typically ranging from 40 to 52 weeks. Sourcing is likely a mix of domestic and international vendors, requiring an assessment of import duties and logistics for large, heavy components (crane planning is critical).
key_points: 48-week equipment lead time requires early procurement planning.
20% mechanical room space allocation (within Uptime Institute guidelines).

fire_suppression.name: Fire Suppression & Life Safety
fire_suppression.content: Per NFPA 75 and FM Global Data Sheet 5-4 standards, the IT data halls will utilize a clean agent suppression system (e.g., FM-200 or Novec 1230) with an integrated pre-action sprinkler system in facility support areas. The overall CAPEX is competitive, and life safety compliance (egress, detection, emergency power-off integration) is standard but complex.
key_points: Clean agent suppression in data halls is the industry standard for minimizing asset damage.
$120/sqm suppression CAPEX is a typical estimate.

assumptions: 50 MW IT load is the baseline for capacity calculations.
WRI Aqueduct Water Stress Index is assumed to be 'medium' (not 'high' or 'extremely high') for the region, preventing a No-Go.
Design is for Tier III (N+1 redundancy) per Uptime Institute standards.
key_insights: Climate (ASHRAE Zone 3A) necessitates an energy-intensive hybrid cooling strategy, limiting PUE to 1.32.
Water-Side Economizer enables 2,200 annual free cooling hours, significantly improving on a pure air-cooled design.
High WUE (1.5 L/kWh) due to evaporative cooling is the primary sustainability and regulatory risk.

Thermal resilience is strong with a 20-minute ride-through (exceeding Tier III minimum), but the high Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE) of 1.5 L/kWh presents a notable long-term sustainability and regulatory risk that must be addressed with water recycling initiatives.
